stem:
Eshan sees wriggling mosquito larvae in stagnant water left in an unused clay pot in his courtyard in Thrissur. His teacher says a thin layer of kerosene on the water surface can stop them becoming adults.

Why does the kerosene layer work?

options.text: It makes the water look shiny, so adult mosquitoes refuse to lay more eggs there.
Larvae and pupae must reach air at the surface to breathe; the kerosene film blocks that air contact and disrupts development before adulthood.
Adult mosquitoes also need to dive under the kerosene to breathe, so the layer kills flying adults in the courtyard.
Kerosene is transparent, so air still reaches the larvae and the layer cannot affect breathing.

teacher.key_rationale: Mosquito larvae and pupae live in water but respire air at the surface. A thin oil/kerosene film separates water from air and blocks that breathing, interrupting the life cycle.
